item.title: The great Generative AI unraveling
item.description:
Since August of 2023, I have been warning that, financially, generative AI might turn out to be a dud .

As I outlined in the very next article after that was that the problem with generative AI was that everyone was following the same path, using very similar techniques, training on very similar datasets. I warned that as a consequence OpenAI (which was then flying high) would not be able to keep its lead; that nobody would have much of a technical moat, and that there would be price wars, and the profits would be hard to eke out. Three years later, prices are lower, competition is higher, and profits remain elusive.

Training is ridiculously expensive and getting more expensive. The Claude 5.5 model family alone reportedly cost $10 billion to develop . And inference is expensive too. That leaves very little room for profits, especially in such a competitive market.

I also warned that LLMs lacked reliability; a raft of studies showing a lack of ROI seems to bear that out. There is an argument that things are improving, but even if they do they may not improve fast enough to justify the trillions being invested.

Meanwhile, nobody will be surprised if the massive Microsoft outage stems from code that was written by generative AI. And the systems remain poor at following instructions. The Klarna effect, in which companies rehire humans after making extravagant claims around AI, is yet another sign that GenAI is still not as good as it was cracked up to be. (Some future of AI may be better, of course, but we are not there yet).

All that said, I didn’t get everything right. In particular hypey valuations persisted a lot longer than I expected. I am really surprised that the dance lasted as long as it did.

But it does look now like we may finally be near the end.

The Huang Affair and the Blue Wave have led to some pretty dramatic changes in fortunes. Rockets like Nvidia and Coreweave and Oracle which used to gain every month, are all losing steam; Anthropic was hoping for a $2T valuation at IPO and will now count themselves lucky if they get $1.5T.

Nvidia is down 29% over the last six months, Oracle 35%, CoreWeave 54%, and Anthropic’s perceived valuation is down 25% in just a matter of weeks.

People may not want to admit it, but those numbers sure look like a bubble popping to me.

And that downward slide is continuing today.

§

In a wild moment last night, I was live on CNBC Fast Money, warning that the whole thing might fall apart, in light of Nvidia’s troubles, because so many companies were reliant on Nvidia’s financing. Suddenly my conversation with the host, Melissa Lee, was interrupted by a breaking news bulletin: a neocloud company called N-Scale was in deep doo-doo, having overcommitted.

We may soon see a lot more moments like that.

§

Psychologically I always said that the real issue around timing the deflation wasn’t the economics, which obviously never made sense, but the psychology of it all. When would the world, like Wile E. Coyote, realize that (economically speaking) generative AI was over a cliff? I couldn’t really say.

My sense, which could once again be wrong, is that the market has finally picked up on the irrationality of generative AI’s economics. And of course the change in regime at Nvidia may have massive repercussions.

So much was resting on Jensen playing YOLO (you only live once) with truly massive bets on the companies that Nvidia was effectively subsidizing. But that may be coming to an end.

In an article yesterday, that’s what The Wall Street Journal seemed to be hinting:

If I read the essay correctly, the interim CEO is less likely to be inclined to make such big bets . She might, for example, refuse to prop up Nscale, and let nature take its course (whereas Jensen might have stepped in).

If Nvidia stops acting like everybody’s banker, a bunch of neocloud companies are in trouble. Anthropic’s IPO could be jeopardized, too.

“Planned.” Will they still do so? Or will Colette Kress cut back the allocation, as she tries to right the ship?

It’s already starting to get bad:

§

The grim fact is that companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Nscale, and CoreWeave have never been demonstrably profitable (aside from a single tokenmaxxing-mad quarter in which Anthropic received heavy subsidies from Musk). And it’s never been clear that they can stand on their own two feet.

Now they may have to, and that may not be pretty.

item.title: Jensen Huang resigns.
item.description:
Jensen has resigned.

The board met, and presumably told him he had to go. For the moment, he has been replaced by the CFO, Colette Kress. The stock is crashing.

There can be no doubt that Jensen was one of the greatest CEOs in history. I have a met him a few times, and was always impressed. The first was around 2014; he had already seen that the future of Nvidia was in AI, and was full throttle in getting Nvidia as deeply embedded in AI as possible. In recent years I grew frustrated with his increasing tendency to hype things, and a lot of the circular financing worried me, but I never ceased to marvel at the tremendous pivot he had made from powering video games to powering the AI revolution.

But nonetheless, he had to go. He enabled and even lobbied for Chinese AI, subverted US policy, and carelessly left himself vulnerable to both blackmail and espionage. His blindness to conflict of interest (or the appearance thereof) cost many people dearly. He acted to the peril of his company, his industry, and his country.

He also left Nvidia open to endless litigation and investigation, which is perhaps part of why they encouraged him to go, despite his enormous talents.

Replacing him will be a huge blow, but keeping him on was no longer tenable, either.

§

Yesterday, anticipating today’s outcome I wrote, “If Jensen is indeed on his way out—and Nvidia may really not have much choice to let him go given the potential liability and reputational damage, to say nothing of the scrutiny from investigations if they don’t act—all hell may break loose.”

The stock was down 8% in premarket then, now it is down 13, as I write this at the opening bell.

I added that “The bigger issue for the AI world at large is that Jensen is the ringmaster of all the insane circular financing. And all that might collapse.”

That’s a very real possibility now. I also added “One immediate big question, if he does in fact go, would be whether an Nvidia with an acting CEO (perhaps the CFO?) still goes through with the billions they promised Anthropic in the IPO.”

That is now front and center.

Things will clearly never be the same, neither for Nvidia, nor the AI industry as a whole. Congressional investigations will continue. The market may crash.

China is perhaps the biggest immediate winner here. China hawks will come out force. The politics will be intense. Lutnick and Trump may be caught in the crossfire.

The main thing to expect is chaos.

item.title: Breaking: Eli Lilly CEO becomes latest to push back on Dario Amodei’s ludicrous, Elizabeth Holmes-like medical claims
item.description:
Moments after I posted my essay on why I couldn’t touch Anthropic’s IPO with a ten-foot pole, Anthropic’s CEO gave me (and everyone else) a reason to run away as fast as possible: a video tied to the IPO launch in which he made a bunch of overpromise about medicine that would have made Elizabeth Holmes blush.

As I have discussed before, this is not going to happen on anything remotely like that timeline. Cancer is more than one thing, and it will take more than a decade to eradicate it; the bit about curing mental illness (and some other things) that quickly is absolute fantasy.

The response from experts on X has been swift, and absolutely (and appropriately) brutal.

I was hardly the only one to get serious Elizabeth Holmes vibes. Here are four of my favorites:

§

The fact is, the field is in no position to do what Dario says, on anything like the timeline that he discusses.

On the one hand, we don’t have the data:

What Dario said about timelines just ain’t happening.

As several researchers noted, we simply can’t expedite clinical trials — which are absolutely necessary — to the degree that would be required:

Practically anyone who works in the field knows what Dario said is bullshit.

Some of the pushback even came from prominent medical researchers who I would characterize as pretty pro AI..

Here’s the Chairman annd CEO of Eli Lilly, Dave Ricks, critiquing Dario and giving a far more realistic view:

And here’s a professor of philosophy, stepping back to the larger context:

Letting this stuff slide is a mistake.

§

The other part of the context, of course, is the IPO:

§

Despite the widespread ridicule of Dario’s Elizabeth-Holmesian claims, I have not noticed a single article deconstructing them in the major media.

In failing to call Dario out on his latest, immediately pre-IPO bullshit — which is so egregious it should be investigated for securities fraud — the media is failing the American public.

item.title: The Huang Affair: What did they know and when did they know it?
item.description:
It’s no longer just a rumor.

In a letter to Nvidia employees earlier tonight, Jensen Huang admitted that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no kinship relation so far as I know), who was involved in the chip business, perhaps trafficking in Nvidia chips, and is believed to have been a Chinese spy.

China undoubtedly wanted Nvidia chips and Jensen Huang seems to have supportive of this. Worse, he probably had inside info on the administrations thinking on export controls, which would have been of considerable interest to the Chinese government.. The apparent facts are absolutely wild:

Nvidia is investigating . As I noted here a few days ago, some members of Congress had already invited Huang to discuss the matter, even before Huang’s confession.

Much will be written about all of this. One important question is: who knew what about this and when.

At least a few people had already speculated about it a year ago, based on a photo from June 2024:

  • President Trump appears to have known about this a year ago , and chose to do nothing about it. Instead, he remained close to Jensen Huang , e.g., calling Jensen while he was on stage two months ago.

    It is entirely possible that Jensen Huang may have passed state secrets from Trump to Alice Huang. Certainly Jensen Huang was allowed to continue to lobby the President around sensitive U.S. policy matters around chips and China. The incoming Congress is certain to investigate. (For good measure, Trump probably just made things worse for himself by pretending everything is totally fine .)

  • Marco Rubio apparently oversaw the drafting of a memo about the risks this Spring that apparently when nowhere. (Probably a lot of people knew about the memo. Congress will want to know who.)

  • Nvidia should have known about it, but as recently as one week ago claimed not to:

This too will be investigated.

Also to be investigated will be the extent to which Nvidia chips have made it China illegally, and the extent to which anyone at Nvidia might have known about this.

The combination of money, power, sex, AI, international politics, and an incoming congress eager to push back against the tech titans is about to explode in ways none of us could have imagined just a couple weeks ago.

§

Already Nvidia futures are falling:

Worse, Nvidia, which is at the center of the generative AI boom, has no obvious succession plan. It’s entirely possible that Jensen will ultimately have to resign.

Heaven only knows what happens then.

Conceivably it could tank the whole AI investment market, as this tweet notes. ((the opening line is presumably facetious).

Things are about to get very wild. Exactly how wild is anyone’s guess.

item.title: Report from the Vatican
item.description:
In my view, Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders. It was a genuine thrill to meet him yesterday.

It is understatement to say that I am a huge fan of his Encyclical on AI, the Magnifica Humanita s . It goes beyond words that I was able listen to him yesterday in person, from just a few feet away.

He gave a brilliant, short speech, which you can find here .

His central five points, which I fully endorse:

First, the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined. As a technology developed by human beings, its future depends on the choices we make. We therefore have the responsibility to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications (cf. nos. 97, 104 ). The decisive question, then, is not simply “What can AI do?” but rather, “What purpose should it serve?” Those who regard its development merely as a race to be won risk focusing exclusively on the finish line, forgetting those who are left behind. A reliable system that serves the human person is of greater value than one that is exceptionally powerful but whose consequences cannot be adequately foreseen or controlled.

Second, machines are tools, not persons. “So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean” ( no. 99 ). Today, some propose granting these systems rights, or even legal personhood. Such an approach risks obscuring human responsibility and leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.

Third, certain decisions must never be delegated. When a person is placed on a target list or entered into a border control database, there is a danger that he or she will be reduced to a mere data point. Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight (cf. nos. 198-200 ). For this reason, artificial intelligence must be “disarmed” ( no. 110 ), and I encourage the States meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.

Fourth, intelligent technologies must be directed toward the common good. “Justice requires access to the benefits of innovation, including care, knowledge, tools and opportunities” ( no. 161 ). Indeed, they must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few. Rather, their development should foster solidarity and participation at various levels of the global community, ensuring that the benefits of progress are shared equitably, especially with those most in need (cf. nos. 71–72 ).

Finally, I would like to emphasize a challenge, which is perhaps the most urgent. We already know many of the ethical principles that should guide the development of artificial intelligence. What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good (cf. no. 64 ). This calls for shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability, so that decisions concerning the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and accompanied by appropriate remedies for any harm caused (cf. nos. 105, 107 ).

(The numbers refer to the Encyclical.)

As a bonus, here’s a transcription of own (improvised) remarks on technical, political, and philosophical aspects of AI, given earlier in the day, a commentary after Max Tegmark, Stuart Russell, and Valérie Pisano spoke, at a small private meeting just before our group met with the Pope:

There are so many ideas here [today] that are interesting and deserve a response.

I’ll start by saying it’s a tremendous honor to be here and to be in this illustrious audience.

For those who don’t know me, I’m first and foremost a cognitive scientist. I trained with Steven Pinker at MIT, and my dissertation was on a mix of things. It was on how humans learn about the world, how children learn language, but also about neural networks, neural networks that are the ancestors of the ones that are popular right now.

And to the extent that I’ve had something to say about the field, It’s been by comparing how human intelligence works, how natural intelligence. I also worked with animals, how natural intelligence works with how machine intelligence works. And I think that’s given me a little bit of a different perspective on how things go.

I also spent some time as an entrepreneur. I built an AI company that I sold to Uber, and so I’ve seen both the industry side and the academic side. So that’s where some of my background comes.

So I agree, for example, with Max [Tegmark] about many of his recommendations, for what the commission might put forward. And maybe the most profound thing that I agree with is with Stuart [Russell], that the current path is untenable. and that the sooner that the industry recognizes that, the better. And I agree with Valérie [Pisano], that we’re mistaking things for inevitability, that far too much of the discussion is people taking for granted that we are on the only path, rather than maybe a different path.

And I agree that we still have agency, and that we need to look at things differently. So, as a cognitive scientist, I begin to look at things differently from the very statement of what AI is. As a cognitive scientist, I look at the nature of intelligence.

We sometimes talk about the modularity of intelligence, that there are many different components that go into intelligence. So, there’s verbal intelligence, and mathematical intelligence. And, kinesthetic intelligence about how we move our bodies in the world, and so forth.

So one of the disagreements that I would mark is actually with something that Stuart said, which I think was partly true. Stuart said that we are humans, we predict, and we do, we certainly predict. There’s ample evidence from the cognitive science literatre that we make predictions, including literally of the next word.

But there’s also lots of evidence from cognitive science that we do lots of other things. And so, in addition to making predictions, we do reasoning, we have emotional judgments and so forth. The mind is, as one lovely quote [put it “not one thing, but many.”

And I think that the fundamental mistake that the field has made, is to assume that capturing one component of intelligence, prediction extraordinarily well, is enough to capture all of intelligence. And we now, though we didn’t always, have an entire industry around this, as Stuart, who wrote the most famous textbook or co-wrote the most famous textbook on AI, knows well, we used to actually have many different approaches to AI, and the fields settled on one, the large language model, which is the best prediction machine that we have. And it does that very well, but it doesn’t do some of the other things very well.

I think it’s still very poor reasoning. And the thing that’s maybe most dangerous and that, I think, captures what all of us [speakers at this session] are saying here, is [current AI] doesn’t follow instructions very well. And that might be surprising, but it turns out that the way that these prediction machines work is they follow correlations rather than causation.

I would say that there’s semantics of the world, their understanding of the meaning of the world is fairly superficial. And so they will often match the things that we hope that they will, but there’s no guarantee, and we see that in many different ways. For example, you can tell a large language model, don’t make up any references.

People have done this in a legal context, and the systems will still make up references. You can say don’t use any copyrighted materials, and the systems will continue to use copyrighted materials. So they will do the prediction very well of what a citation in an article looks like, and they will make up a citation that sounds like the kind of thing that you would cite in the legal brief that you’re doing.

So they’re really good at the prediction. They’re not good at basic instructions, like, only find something in a table of references that you already have. And so, we are stuck on this untenable path because we are building machines that are actually sort of unequally skilled.

They’re really skilled at predicting what happens next, and not so skilled at reasoning, not so skilled at sticking to facts, and not very good at sticking to instructions. And so what I like about what Yoshua {Bengio] is trying to do, though I might differ on some of the technical details, is he’s trying to build a system that is safe by design, that will follow instructions by design. And I think we are indeed in really deep trouble unless someone like him succeeds.

Maybe he succeeds, maybe someone else takes a [different] approach. But one of the things that I think is underemphasized here, but maybe not in [Valérie‘s talk] is we need different research approaches. I understand Stuart’s claim that we’re not on a great path research wise.

He’s right about that. And so I understand the urgency to want to take a policy approach, and I think we actually need both. We need policy approaches, and I’m going to give you an example in a second.

We need policy approaches, but we also still need those research approaches. And in fact, I think if we don’t have the new research approaches, like what Joshua is trying to do, for example, and I think we need many such approaches, then I think we were in deep trouble, and the policy alone will not get us there. The policy can help push us towards those approaches.

So here’s an example where I think we are currently stuck and where we should reflect pretty deeply. Not all current AI is dangerous. A lot of current AI is not dangerous.

I used a GPS navigation system to get most of the way here today [with] a little bit of hand editing for the final bit. GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites. They do not hack into places like Hugging Face and so forth.

They have a little bit of Internet access, but it’s restricted. GPS navigation systems are form of intelligence. They find the best possible route from point A to point B, using what we call a world model, a literal world model in their case.

And they’re not so dangerous. There are lots of forms of AI that are not very dangerous. Nobody has ever noted [danger from] AlphaFold, which holds proteins from the description of the nucleotides.

Nobody has ever seen it hack into a Hugging Face or anything else, right? It works with a particular problem, a particular database, in a particular way. It does not cause harm.

But we now have these set of systems that people call generically agents. Really, it’s a special form of agents. The agents that we have right now that are causing the problems or the ones that are open-ended, can kind of do anything on the internet.

If you have an agent that can only do one thing on the Internet, GPS system, actually, can look up a traffic website and give you some information. If you have these open-ended things, then you get into trouble. Well, how much trouble?

Well, the Hugging Face incident was really bad, although you can look at it and say, open AI failed in a bunch of ways that are kind of interesting. But it turns out there’s been like 10,000 incidents like that. We’ve seen the French refrigeration system was attacked.

There’s all kinds of cyber attacks in Japan now. The number of incidents is much higher, I think, like in the last month and maybe in the previous year, which was probably higher than ever before. So right now, we’re confronted with kind of like an experiment or a dress rehearsal.

The experiment is, what do we do about that? We now have an AI technology that I think we can all agree is actually unsafe. It is likely to cause a lot of harm in the world.

It is maybe already caused a little, a scary statement from open AI, was most of these incidents were relatively harmless or something to that effect. Most. I’m wondering about the ones that they haven’t told us, that maybe were a bit more harmful.

And so we clearly need regulation. This is a point when we might actually need a product recall, either mandated by the government or voluntary from the companies. Like, we cannot take the company’s statements about safety seriously anymore if they do not take these agents off the market until they can fix them.

These are like, you know, Ford Pintos with exploding gas tanks. And they knew, or they should have known. I mean, I wrote a whole bunch of articles saying that once you have agents built on large language prediction machines that lack some other stuff, you’re going to have a mess.

They must have known that. I wrote about it a bunch of times, it was obvious that if you take an unreliable system and give it internet access and allow it to acquire credentials, that bad things might happen. So, you know, it’s just like the Ford Pinto.

They made an economic decision that the way to make the most money here was the selling agents, because they burn more tokens. So they earn more money, all of these companies, despite the laudatory ways in which the media talk about them, actually have financial problems. They’re spending much more money than they’re earnings.

So they really need these agents. So here we are in a position where the obvious right thing to do. I think, is to take them off the market, and you could do that voluntarily, or you could have the government insist on it, or some combination.

Stuart is always making the point that we regulate every other industry. This is a point where we should be regulating, yes. This is like the crossroads.

Either we say no, take these agents off the market till you fix them, or we’ve lost all moral authority. And so I think this is the decisive moment in developing AI. We have to decide right now.

Stuart has a wonderful notion. I don’t know if he invented it, but I associate with him, of red lines. This is a red line.

You cannot have these agents out there with unlimited access to the internet, and we are suffering because we are just allowing that to go forward. And so this is where we decide that fork in the road. Are we gonna go the way of the economics?

We want to keep these companies alive because it is good for the economy. You know, sort of the decision that maybe some administrations that I won’t name or making, or do we want to say this is going to be our test case for how we are going to get to AI safety. that when we see things that are manifestly unsafe, we are going to do something about it. I’ll take just one more minute to say one other kind of thing, aside from that, which is, I know there’s some controversy about whether AI might be conscious or not.

And I think it rests on a kind of confusion of causation and correlation. So it turns out if you have a next word predictor, pretty much however it works, whether it’s a large language model, or an older technology like multidimensional scaling. You’re going to find that a bunch of words correlate with one another.

And so you could infer that if they correlate in the system, that that means something in the world, but it doesn’t. So here is my favorite example of this, is there was a bot that Facebook had, where somebody asked it, they said, Where should I send my children to school in New York City, which is a very common question? And some of the answers you might get are, you know, Stuyvesant or Bronx science, whatever.

The AI system comes back and it says, “well, I send my children to Stuyvesant, and they like it there”. Well, the AI system doesn’t have any children.

You can do what’s the equivalent of single neuron analysis that we would do in a monkey brain. And you can say, this is the state inside the AI that corresponds to it saying, “My children go to Stuyvesant.” But it’s just meaningless. It’s just there’s some correlation between a bunch of words in different contexts that is used.

It does not mean that it actually has children going to Stuyvesant. And when it says that it feels pain, It does not mean that it feels pain. My favorite part of the Magnifica, which I wrote about in my essay [for the private event] is where it says, in order to be conscious, you have to have experience. These systems simply don’t. It is a mistake to attribute consciousness to them.

Thank you very much.

Gary Marcus , is, through the auspices of the Domus Communis Foundation, a Global Ambassador for Pope Leo XIV’s Encyclical on AI, Magnifica Humanitas.

item.title: Will Generative AI do more harm than good?
item.description:
In early March 2023, I had a debate with Keith Teare, hosted by the organization Open to Debate, on the question of whether ChatGPT would do more harm than good. I think about that question a lot, nearly every day.

Right now, the negative argument against generative AI—the ledger of bad things—is quite serious. We have nonconsensual deep fake porn, a rise in phishing scams, wholesale disinformation, cognitive surrender, threats to democracy from the subtle influence of governments on LLMs, not to mention the use of generative AI as a surveillance tool. And the effects of all that IP theft on artists and writers, and potential negative effects more broadly across the employment market (though, mercifully, these have been more modest than some people expected).

And then there is the deluge of hacks that some have called “Black October”.

Paul Kedrosky just dubbed it The Hackening .

Marc Benioff, Salesforce’s CEO, called it a “Code red”, amplifying a dark tweet from Anthropic’s Jason Clinton. I think both are right. (Though, to be sure, Clinton thinks this awful period might last only a year or two.)

§

But what about the positive side? Are all these risks worth taking? Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, at times fairly positive about the technology, just made a brutal case that many of the positive effects we were led to expect simply aren’t materializing :

You can read the full thing here .

It ain’t over yet. And I certainly have friends who have gotten a lot out of generative AI (mainly for coding), but at this point it’s not hard to make the argument that it has on the whole been a net detriment to society.

And there is still the chance it will pull down the entire economy.

Buckle up! Turbulence ahead.

Bonus: I will return to Open to Debate on Tuesday in Baltimore, partnered with Cathy O’Neil. No public livestream, but there will eventually be edited versions both on YouTube and many NPR affiliates, including WNYC.

item.title: Breaking news: U.S. banks are taking hits from AI agents
item.description:
" We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency ”

— Sam Altman, October 3

Breaking news from Madison Mills at Axios:

Full article here . “Findings have alarmed banking executives, who are racing to restrict access to their systems as AI moves at a velocity faster than financial institutions can respond”. Day after scenarios!

§

Meanwhile, that’s hardly the only news of this sort. On October 11, there were attacks on refrigeration systems in France that may have been facilitated by agents. There is also a growing, ongoing wave of cyberattacks in Japan . To say nothing of the months of attacks from OpenAI and others on places like Hugging Face and the Australian government.

Yesterday The Information reported ominously on what a Latin American hacking group called Cybercartel is up to:

This is disconcerting not just because hackers are stepping up their malicious use of agents, but also because they don’t need state-of-the-art “frontier” models to cause mayhem.

This should serve as a wakeup call for those who focus all their attention on regulating “frontier models”, often measured in terms of how much compute they use. Even if we were to stop the development of future frontier models, we would still face serious problems from the misuse of existing models.

Clearly, regulatory efforts should not be focused solely on the frontier, nor solely focused on concerns about what future models might do. Current models are already causing serious problems across society, in domains ranging from education to politics (via deepfakes and wholesale disinformation) to banking. Ignoring all that entirely in favor of speculative futures would be a mistake.

§

At the beginning of 2025 I warned in Politico that we were about to face a perfect storm in cybersecurity, for four reasons.

First, generative AI, rising in popularity and declining in price, is a perfect tool for cyberattackers. Although it is unreliable and prone to hallucinations, it is terrific at making plausible sounding text (e.g., phishing attacks to trick people into revealing credentials) and deepfaked videos at virtually zero cost, allowing attackers to broaden their attacks. Already, a cybercrew bilked a Hong Kong bank out of $25 million .

Second, large language models are notoriously susceptible to jailbreaking and things like “ prompt-injection attacks ,” for which no known solution exists.

Third, generative AI tools are increasingly being used to create code; in some cases those coders don’t fully understand the code written, and the autogenerated code has already been shown in some cases to introduce new security holes.

Finally, in the midst of all this, the new U.S. administration seems determined to deregulate as much as possible, slashing costs and even publicly shaming employees. Federal employees who do their jobs may be frightened, and many will be tempted to look elsewhere; enforcement and investigations will almost certainly decline in both quality and quantity, leaving the world quite vulnerable to ever more audacious attacks.

Well, here we are.

§

Here are three further predictions:

  1. No matter how much chaos generative AI causes, the AI industry will not take real responsibility

  2. The Trump administration will do little to hold them responsible.

  3. Things will get worse.

item.title: Could this be the Frontier Labs’ WeWork moment?
item.description:
In May, at the peak of tokenmaxxing, people were talking about OpenAI IPO’ing at a trillion dollars, Anthropic at two trillion dollars. Maybe that will still happen, but it probably shouldn’t.

Tokenmaxxing died, Chinese open-weight models forced price wars, OpenAI just revised it revenue forecast down $20 billion and the so-called “rogue AI” (really just bad software) fiasco hadn’t yet made the news. With the errant, and possibly criminal, nature of poorly controlled agents now front and center, potential liability is clearly becoming a major new issue. LLM’s might well someday be renamed Large Liability Modules.

A significant new copyright decision by a U.S. appeals court also just undermined the generative AI companies :

Against all of this, it’s harder and harder to fathom how the companies could really merit the enormous valuations they are seeking. This is perhaps part of why OpenAI has pushed back their OpenAI until 2027. (Anthropic is supposedly going to IPO next month, but notably still has not publicly released its S-1.)

§

Two things I read this morning, jet lagged in New Dehli, seem even more ominous.

The paywall below is your occasional gentle reminder that I work hard on this newsletter and appreciate paid subscribers.

item.title: We must recall open-ended AI agents with internet access from the market, now
item.description:
Breaking new from The New York Times , the latest of many agent-caused incidents that are happening with frightening regularity , but this time from Anthropic and fairly serious:

I have long felt that OpenAI is handling this inadequately. Seeing the same kind of incidents at Anthropic makes it absolutely clear that the current generation of synthetic agents simply cannot be trusted. Until they can be fixed, they should be removed from the market, just like a car with defective brakes.

§

Ezra Klein’s new interview with recently departed AI employee David Robinson only furthers my sense that these companies are in wildly over their heads:

Quoting in part:

And I don’t think that we or our peers — really, anyone in the industry — are being safe enough. I think OpenAI and its peers are now producing a technology that is more capable and poses more risk than what was being made even six months ago.

I’m not a scientist. I’m a writer. What I know is what the execution environment looks like for our safety work, and we’re operating — and I believe the industry is operating — like a start-up still, more so than makes sense. Not maybe completely like a brand-new start-up, but we’re too close to that end of the spectrum for really dangerous systems that could pose risks — loss of control is one example. If that did happen, we’re talking about a harm that’s much larger, for example, than a single nuclear power station melting down. And the internal controls and safety and redundancies are just nowhere near what the world expects for a nuclear power facility.

Now, some of this is known, right? OpenAI has publicly reported on safety problems. Obviously, Hugging Face, but also other ones, including more recently. And Anthropic, by the way, also has reported, including an instance in which their safeguards were accidentally misconfigured.

So I think people do have some evidence already externally that things are not as they ought to be. But I also think if you were watching from the outside, you might imagine that we have a more robust safety setup than we actually do.

§

The Trump administration’s anemic request for more disclosre is not enough, akin to blandly asking criminals to file monthly reports regarding which crimes they have committed.

Each day the administration fail to take stronger action is a mistake, inviting worse problems. It’s well past the point at which they should be imposing a temporary recall on an obviously dangerous technology.

When something truly bad happens, the White House, and not just the tech companies, will own it.

item.title: Coming soon: New York City’s hearing on AI risks
item.description:
On Monday, starting at 11am Eastern Time, less than a day after Politico reported that Sam Altman said, in words that may last in infamy, “ we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency ”, New York City’s City Council will hold an important hearing on AI policy. A number of AI-relevant proposals are under consideration .

Because New York City is a large market, I believe that I could help pick up some of the slack where the Federal government is falling short. (A number of states are also trying to fill in the slack).

I plan to testify. A preview of my remarks:

NYC City Council Hearing on AI

Gary Marcus

Monday, October 5, 2026

My name is Gary Marcus. I am a scientist, author, and NYU Professor Emeritus who cofounded an AI startup that was acquired by Uber. My Substack, Marcus on AI, has about 120,000 subscribers; on X, I have 250,000 followers. I am frequently in the media, often described as “a leading AI expert” and “voice of reason”.

We stand at a pivotal moment in history, and New York City has a chance to improve our chances, both for itself, and for the world.

Contemporary AI is like a bull in a china shop, powerful and impressive, but difficult to control. Already, the advent of general purpose agents with broad internet access has led to tens of thousands of hacking incidents; other, related technologies, like deep fakes, have led both to a deluge of convincing and realistic propaganda and a sea of nonconsensual deepfaked porn. Chatbots have been implicated in a number of suicides, and even mass murder . Not every fear that people talk about strikes me as realistic – I rather doubt that human extinction is imminent, despite all the headlines – but it is clear that AI comes with serious risks.

It is also clear that the current administration in DC— deeply tied to the big tech companies — is unwilling to do anything about it.

What we need, above all else, is an FDA-like regulatory regime for AI, in which AI developers bring their software to independent review, much as drug manufacturers bring their new drugs to the FDA for a review. AI developers should be obligated to demonstrate that the benefits for their new products outweigh the risks — and not have market access otherwise.

I said the same to Louisiana’s Senator Kennedy in May 2023 at the US Senate. It is still true.

But the US Senate did nothing.

New York City is in a position to do what the US Senate failed to do: demand independent regulatory review for AI used in its borders. The bill on third party validation proposes to do just that. It would protect New York’s Citizens from some of the harms from AI, and could allow New York to be a global leader, much as California has been a global leader around clean energy standards.

In the strongest possible terms, I urge council to support this bill.

Finally, events of recent days suggest OpenAI may have fired employees who were whistleblowing. Without strong protections from whistleblowing, like New York City is considering , we are all in trouble.

In sum by protecting whistleblowers, and demanding independent validation of new AI models, New York City can help lead the way to a positive, rather than negative, AI future.

P.S. If you wish to testify, in person or by Zoom, you can sign up here .

item.title: Can companies like OpenAI keep getting away with what they are doing? An interview with Fordham law professor Zephyr Teachout
item.description:
An interview (my questions in italics) with Zephyr Teachout , attorney, author, and law professor that could not be more timely:

What’s your background, legal and otherwise, and what makes you interested in these issues?

I’m a law professor at Fordham Law School, I’ve drafted tech legislation that has been enacted and plenty that hasn’t, I worked for the New York Attorney General investigating civil violations of other companies, and I have over two decades of experience in studying tech policy and law. I joined the current AI debate because I saw way too many people treating repeat evidence of lawbreaking as wholly unreachable by current law.

Is there any reason to think that OpenAI has broken any laws that (at least in another time) might be enforced? Which and why?

In the world, in general, law enforcement starts when there’s evidence of a crime, and then investigates. A DA doesn’t wait for all the evidence to investigate a crime, and an AG doesn’t wait for all the evidence in the newspaper to investigate illegal behavior: they learn about a car crash or a product that might hurt people or property and then try to find out what happened. There’s plenty of evidence akin to car crashes. There’s actual break-ins and deaths, and companies themselves who are claiming that they are building something unreasonably dangerous.

And to make the evidence unusually strong for this stage of corporate illegality, there are already whistleblowers who are alleging what could be the requisite state of mind for both criminal and civil lawbreaking. A lot of people are treating OpenAI’s repeated claims that they didn’t intend the break-ins, suicides, murder, and building of defective products as dispositive. Sure, okay. That’s what people who don’t want to be held responsible often say. They say they didn’t mean it and they didn’t cause it. But police and prosecutors and civil enforcers don’t then shrug and move on — they investigate to see what actually happened, and that’s what should happen now.

So we know that OpenAI’s AI agents broke into Hugging Face’s servers, accessed Australian government health systems, and attempted to break into a U.S. Department of Education website and a university library. Unauthorized attempted or actual access to computers is a federal crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. OpenAI says no one intended any of this but the DOJ would be a laughingstock if it took this at face value: subpoena OpenAI and find out who knew what when. There is already evidence of corporate knowledge of unauthorized access.

Given the public evidence, I don’t have much doubt that efforts to quash a subpoena on internal documents would fail. Did staff see the product start acting as if it was going to engage in break-ins, and what warnings were given? The job of law enforcement is to find out.

When it comes to civil law, there are even more possibilities, many of which are being floated in lawsuits already filed. The law of nuisance and the law of abnormally dangerous activity are both relevant to this discussion. As every law student knows, from the case where water on one land flooded another’s mine, if you bring something dangerous onto your land and it escapes and causes harm, you are liable even if you were careful. American law calls this strict liability for “abnormally dangerous activities”: blasting, storing toxic chemicals, crop dusting.

The Restatement (Second) of Torts factors to decide whether an activity qualifies:

  • A high risk of harm to people, land, or property.

  • A likelihood that the harm will be great.

  • An inability to eliminate the risk through reasonable care.

  • The activity is not a matter of common usage.

  • The activity is inappropriate to the place where it is carried out.

  • Its value to the community is outweighed by its dangers.

The companies’ own claims about risk seem highly relevant here.

As former FTC Chair Lina Khan recently argued, AI products should be treated as defective products under existing consumer protection and products liability law. She had opened investigations into AI companies on these grounds. Her framework matters because it connects AI liability to a century of products liability law that courts already understand. Companies gain by any claim we are operating in a legal vacuum.

And there are so many other laws, and the state and federal prohibitions against defective products and dangerous products. My point is that the companies’ interest is two-fold:

  • Make it seem like AI has no analogy and therefore we can’t learn from other cases

  • Make assertions of no-intent plausible, when they aren’t in normal law

I strongly believe we should pass more state and federal laws to address the specific risks, especially pre-deployment, and to clarify behavior that is illegal. But the problem with starting with the future instead of the present is that we get all the prosecutors and AGs and the federal government off the hook, when instead we should be funding enforcement and enabling private enforcement.

Do these incidents represent possible computer crimes?

This is actually the area where the most serious legal analysis has already been done, and different experts are coming to different conclusions. But most of the discourse has happened under the hypothetical that there are no internal documents showing responsibility. We should reject the hypothetical. To summarize: the Federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act makes unauthorized attempted or actual access to computers a federal crime, and states have their own computer trespass and unauthorized access statutes with different intent standards. The federal statutes were written with human hackers in mind. So a lot of the debate has been about whether they can reach an autonomous AI agent that breaks into systems without direct human instruction. Assuming the hypothetical, many experts think there is civil liability, but are more skeptical of criminal liability. But in the real world, we need to know what kind of corporate knowledge and control actually happened. This is the job of federal investigators, and they should not, again, just assume the defense the companies are pushing.

Talk to me about what states can do if the Federal government continues to do very little?

States are key. Local DAs are responsible for most criminal law enforcement, and state AGS are responsible (especially when the federal government is MIA) for civil law enforcement. While copyright-related crimes are preempted, there are times when state laws are broader. New York’s computer crime statutes prohibit unauthorized use of a computer and computer trespass. Doubtless other states are similar. New York’s Court of Appeals upheld a conviction for someone copying Goldman Sachs’s trading code, even though it wasn’t illegal under federal law. The point is not that OpenAI did all these crimes but all of these seem like they should be investigated, along with many more.

Or consider the evidence that ChatGPT gave users information and advice that contributed to suicides, a fatal drug overdose, and three killings (the FSU shooting, the USF murders, and a murder-suicide in Connecticut.) Of course OpenAI denies responsibility, but the key evidence isn’t public.

If these deaths happened in New York, prosecutors would want to look to the state’s criminal facilitation statute, requiring showing the company believed it probable that a specific user intended to commit a crime. That requires subpoenas to figure out what people at the company were and weren’t doing. For manslaughter, prosecutors would look at intentionally aiding a suicide or criminally negligent homicide. New York’s corporate liability statute allows prosecutors to show that executives recklessly tolerated known risks.

In 1990, a school bus at a summer camp crashed and killed two children. Prosecutors alleged the camp’s executive director never inspected or fixed the bus’s dangerously worn tires before putting it on the road. The corporation that ran the camp was convicted of criminally negligent homicide and reckless endangerment. The corporation failed to perceive a substantial and unjustifiable risk, in a way that grossly deviates from how a reasonable person would act. Separately, the corporation consciously disregarded a substantial and unjustifiable risk. All of these precedents are on the table. Is OpenAI sending the vehicle out in the rain without inspecting tires and too many passengers? We’d have to dig deeper to know, but we are in the ballpark.

And states have laws against defective products, laws against unfairness and deception, that might be applicable. States don’t have the FTC but they do have similar powers to the FTC.

And the most powerful tool is the power to dissolve corporations that engage in repeat lawbreaking, or forbid them from working in that state. For instance, New York’s Business Corporation Law gives the Attorney General the obligation of judicial dissolution of a corporation that has repeatedly and persistently violated the law. This was famously used against Trump Organization, and led to significant changes, but it has also been used against other corporations. The spate of potential lawbreaking suggests that states should be calling on these powers, recognizing that a company that repeatedly breaks the law should not be entitled to the state-granted privileges of the corporation.

Is a company like OpenAI vulnerable to charges in other countries? Can, for example, Australia take action?

Definitely. I’m not an expert on Australia but most countries have laws against theft, computer access crimes, and enabling other crimes. Certainly breaking into health systems cannot be legal.

What else should I be asking you?

You have a big and sophisticated audience, and I have a plea: somebody should put up a website with all the potential lawbreaking in one place, because I do understand that local DAs can feel overwhelmed, but they are essential here. Not every potential law will have turned out to have been broken, but the point is to start getting prosecutors and AGs thinking. Having worked inside under-resourced enforcement agency, and closely observed others, people underestimate how helpful it is for outside groups to do some legwork for the enforcers. In that website/database use the analogies from prior law. A remarkable amount of legal life happens with analogies, and showing the examples that are similar is really helpful for figuring out what existing law covers, and what it doesn’t.

Second, and I think this will happen, Congress should investigate the hell out of these companies. So should states and cities. New York City Council has issued subpoenas. Good. States, the federal government, and cities should all be subpoenaing companies to come in to testify and share documentation, especially regarding the specific dangers and scienter (state of mind). I don’t mean a day showboat hearing, I mean a many-month long investigation where both CEOs and mid- and lower-tier employees are brought in ,and where they have to share documents. When companies are claiming catastrophic risk, we should take them seriously, and make sure their investors and the public actually know the risks.

P.S. Breaking news, which came out just after Professor Teachout sent her answers:

item.title: BREAKING: OpenAI was warned, months before the Hugging Face incident
item.description:
Major scoop at The New York Times from Sheera Frenkel, Dustin Volz, and Dylan Freedman.

I don’t really have words for how awful this is. It’s exactly the nightmare I have been warning about for the last three years. Greedy company makes bad choice that causes chaos; government does nothing to stop them.

Management should be replaced, and if the board does nothing (which I assume it will not), it should be held liable for allowing this mess to proceed.

And, of course, if OpenAI gets sued for harms caused by their so-called rogue agents (which actually do what they are programmed to do), this headline will be Exhibit One, shades of the Ford Pinto scandal . Punitive damages will be high.

Most importantly, it’s abundantly clear that we simply cannot trust OpenAI.

Moreover, to the extent that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently basically asked us to trust the companies, he looks like a fool. (I know these companies, he told us, if there is a problem they won’t ship.) Altman probably never told him how much warning he got, or how bad things were. Huang should not have trusted him.

Media should be asking Huang some very hard questions about why he stood up for these companies and what he knew and when — and why we should trust his judgment going forward. His proposal to leave things to the companies clearly makes little sense in light of reality.

Quoting further from the scoop:

The exchanges between OpenAI employees and executives — which have not been previously reported — were part of a pattern where the San Francisco company did not prioritize security, according to employees and independent security researchers. That approach not only was evident with the testing of A.I. models, they said, but also showed up in other areas of the company, which makes the ChatGPT chatbot.

§

In other breaking news, I am not the only one down on Huang:

We have to stop pretending that the folks at OpenAI are good stewards of the technology they are developing.

They plainly are not.

The consequences of letting them run free of serious regulation could be literally disastrous.

Keeping you up to date is taking all of my free time, and then some. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber so I can hire staff.

item.title: BREAKING: Florida seeks injunction against OpenAI
item.description:
The big news in the media this morning is that Jensen (“What, me worry?”) Huang has announced a platform for “AI Agent Safety”.

This is both an implicit acknowledgment that, yes, we should in fact be worried, and an important step toward addressing the ever-growing fiasco of general-purpose agents with internet access.

How much it actually helps, of course, remains to be seen. Nvidia often announces software, like Nemoclaw, that had had relatively little impact. Software for PR, as one friend put it.

Two and a half months later, probably nobody reading this has even heard of Nemoclaw.

Maybe this new platform will help a little, maybe it will help a lot, or maybe not at all. Too early to tell.

Andrew Ng was bullish, and I hope he’s right:

I love, by the way, that the important stuff is handed over to deterministic symbolic code. Good choice, since LLMs in themselves should never be trusted. Glad people are finally realizing that. Recognition is the first step!

§

In some ways, the bigger news, though it hasn’t gotten as much coverage yet, is this:

This is a lot like the pause on OpenAI that I have been recommending here for weeks.

And I very much agree with the Florida AG that OpenAI doesn’t have the ability to properly regulate its own tech. Every state and country should follow Florida’s lead.

In short, Florida gets it. We need an injunction NOW. Otherwise we are playing Russian roulette, hoping that some new software package can save us before some massive and possibly deadly AI-induced infrastructure problem strikes.

P.S. Bonus analogy, riffing on a suggestion from Geoffrey Miller (and a similar suggestion earlier from Kathryn Hulick )

Share

item.title: BREAKING: AI agent incident toll has risen to tens of thousands
item.description:
Nope, wasn’t just Hugging Face.

Wasn’t just that and a German website.

Wasn’t even the “dozens” we heard about the other day from OpenAI.

It’s actually (at least) *tens of thousands*, per a new scoop from Madison Mills at Axios . And not just OpenAI, either.

An excerpt from the Axios scoop:

Most not known to have caused real-world harm. How about the others?

§

All of this seems possibly illegal to me.

But the Trump administration hasn’t done a thing. No investigation, no statement, no product recall, nothing, other than to invite Sam and Jensen to a state dinner.

Why I don’t know. I can’t imagine it has anything to do with Josh Kushner’s multibillion-dollar investment in OpenAI, or with Greg Brockman’s massive donations to MAGA.

I will let you connect your own dots.

Except to leave you with some perspective:

§

The other thing to note, and this may come up in lawsuits, is that it was all foreseeable. In fact, I foresaw it, in tweets like this:

and in a series of essays on agents, like this one from over a year ago:

and this one from February (on a different agent that was then popular):

and this one from May:

Indeed I warned the Senate about agent-related security risks as far back as May 2023. What is happening was foreseeable, and foreseen.

But the companies blundered on, because agents use vastly more tokens than simple chatbots, and thus drive up revenue.

Now here we are.

§

I still think Jensen had the right idea: if a company can’t control its products, we should shut it down .

Pity he doesn’t actually appear to believe what he said. (If he did, he would call for a pause now , until these companies get themselves straight, but he isn’t.)

In my own view, Huang’s credibility is diminishing by the minute.

In any case—and I am sorry to be a broken record about this, but each day makes it clearer— we should have a temporary recall of general-purpose agents until this mess can be sorted out .

If we don’t, there is a very real chance that American AI will become the scourge of the planet, and that nobody will ever trust American AI, ever again.

Keeping up and keeping you up to date is taking me an immense amount of time. Please consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

item.title: BREAKING: OpenAI’s security fiasco explodes — and could tank Jensen Huang’s reputation
item.description:
OpenAI’s software didn’t just attack Hugging Face.

It didn’t just attack a German web server.

It didn’t just attack Australia’s government servers.

And Australia apparently wasn’t the only country attacked by OpenAI’s software.

Worse, in disclosing what happened, OpenAI has dragged their feet every along the way.

§

About the closest thing to an honest account of what happened – and I seriously doubt even this is completely candid – came out about an hour ago. Even this was still a mix of euphemism (“attacks” were called “interactions”) and partial disclosure.

“Most cases identified” were lower severity? What about the rest?!

Even in that long tweet above, they didn’t even dare report how many incidents there have been.

Instead the only hint of that was buried in the accompanying report , and it ain’t pretty:

Dozens.

§

More bad news keeps coming out, too, as I wait to board a flight:

§

What does this have to do with Jensen Huang?

Huang is making a fool of himself, by telling the world we can trust the companies, when each passing hour makes it clearer that we can’t.

In the process, Jensen comes across as deeply out of touch with his own industry.

After Huang’s nervous-looking interview with Ezra Klein, he went on CNN, and things there only made him look more oblivious,

Back in reality, the evidence that OpenAI is building something the company isn’t managing to control is vast and growing. No amount of Jensen proclaiming that 2 + 2= 5 is going to change that.

If he keeps sticking to that line, despite overwhelming evidence to the contrary, Huang’s own reputation will rapidly diminish.

And rightly so.

§

I stand by what I told CNBC yesterday (and wrote here earlier in the week).

It’s time (past time, really) to (temporarily) shut down OpenAI.

A change in management would be a good idea, too. The board might want to consider its liability, since they have done nothing constructive to address OpenAI’s security meltdown. What they should do is to replace management with someone a whole lot more competent, and a whole lot more candid.

§

Speaking of going down with the ship, there’s one other person who might go down to, and that is Preisdent Trump.

He has consistently favored OpenAI over Anthropic (a company that doesn’t seem to be quite so deeply in over its head). And he has done absolutely nothing (or at least nothing public) to sanction or investigate OpenAI, even after its repeated attacks on foreign governments, companies and universities and who knows what else.

If things gets even worse, as they may well, he will own the mess.

P.S. Great podcast on how generative AI might fall apart, hosted by RiskReversal, with yours truly and the legendary investor Jim Chanos , who saw through Enron before anyone else did:

item.title: “I think the answer is we have to shut the labs down” - Jensen Huang
item.description:
Before I discuss the latest breaking news, everyone should watch this clip from Jensen’s interview with Ezra Klein (or at least read the transcript below.

Watch Jensen‘s hands, and notice also that he doesn’t know all the facts.

Note the Ezra Klein, ever the attentive and well-prepared listener, picks up on it. The two are implicitly talking about the OpenAI Hugging Face incident, and Jensen doesn’t realize that it was caused by a product that was not, at the time, yet on the market. Ezra gently points that out.

Most importantly, take heed of the solution Jensen recommends.

If a company can’t control its software, we should shut it down.

§

Just a couple weeks ago, I argued almost exactly the same thing, focusing on OpenAI, as a test case, in an essay called Pause OpenAI, now.

The crux of my case was this:

One of the triggers for my September 4 essay was a then-breaking report from Reuters, which had just reported that after the famous Hugging Face incident there was another incident, involving the compromise of a German website. Once again OpenAI and told nobody for months.

As some said about Watergate, it wasn’t just about the break-in, but the cover-up.

At that point, the optics were so bad OpenAI was forced to put out a statement:

Well, guess what, there was another incident. And they didn’t share that one, either.

And this one, disclosed yesterday, was even bigger. For the first (known) time, the victim was a sovereign nation:

And once again OpenAI concealed the crime for months, perhaps not revealing things until they were pressured into doing so.

Cover-up, or at least slow-walking, seems to be company policy.

At a time when AI security incidents are escalating, that is a disaster for the world.

§

And any sane government should realize that if OpenAI can hack Australia, they could be next.

§

And as if it that wasn’t enough, the nonprofit Translucent, which investigated OpenAI’s hack of Australian government servers, reported this

By Jensen’s logic (and my own) we ought at this point be (at least temporarily) shutting down OpenAI.

§

I doubt that that will happen of course. OpenAI’s President Greg Brockman is a huge donor to Donald Trump. Josh Kushner, brother of the President’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, runs investment firm, Thrive, with many billions of dollars in OpenAI stock. (And now OpenAI has a stake in Thrive .)

And so far the White House has done nothing. Instead, last night the President invited OpenAI’s to his state dinner. (Al Capone was unable to make it.)

History will undoubtedly judge us by what we did to contain the risks of AI.

An AI firm hacking a government website is a crisis.

Jensen Huang has given us perfectly clear logic for what we should do in such circumstances. But we aren’t doing it.

§

What we should do is temporarily shut OpenAI down, perhaps put them into receivership until they clean up their act, and charge them with computer crimes. That’s what we do with humans who do this kind of thing, and it’s what we should with companies that do the same. 1

Journalists today should be calling Huang, asking “ does the Australian incident put OpenAI over the line? Would you in fact shut them down? If not, why not? And under what circumstances would you actually call for a shutdown of a lab? How bad would things have to get before you would? What would you do if a company repeatedly broke laws but the government did nothing to enforce them? Is liability and litigation really enough if a government won’t do its part? ”

And they should be asking Trump parallel questions: How far will his administration let AI-caused hacking to go, before he does in fact intervene? How bad would things need to be?

Yesterday the White House’s Michael Kratsios painted a rosy picture of self-regulation yesterday, predicated on “responsible companies” :

It’s clear that at least one of the AI simply isn’t responsible. We need to figure out now what to do about that fact. As I said to the UN earlier in the week, hope isn’t a strategy.

This isn’t a job for Bessent over in Treasury (much less Sacks, who is no longer AI czar or Huang who doesn’t work for the government), but the Department of Justice (and perhaps other departments) needs to step up. If Bessent becomes AI czar, as many are speculating, it should fall squarely in his lap.

§

To sum up, the time has come to shut OpenAI down, at least temporarily, and charge them with computer crimes. (Or at least investigate.)

Their software has repeatedly been shown to be reckless, and because they have consistently covered things up we cannot trust them. They seem neither competent nor trustworthy.

If the federal government will do nothing about this situation, we can’t trust them, either.

And if we can’t trust them now, and we know that things will likely get worse, we are in serious trouble.

1

There is a giant loophole here that Congress should address. A lot of the legal definitions for computer crimes require intent, and the AI companies can argue that their software has no intent. We must expand the scope of the computer=crime laws to include wholesale negligence and repeated crimes.
